near_miss.lead: Man, woman, and sleeping: maðr/kona/svaf versus мужи/женою/спѧть.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse sleeping subject is Ymir; the man and woman grow under his arm. In the chronicle men sleep sexually with one woman. Cognate words have different dependencies and narrative functions.

near_miss.lead: Long life versus short life; langt lif.
near_miss.why_not: Cato measures a rope, not a lifetime. A corpus search finds Vedic dīrghám ā́yuḥ but no qualifying second slab anchor. Long life is also an ordinary wish; the Vedic life noun is not cognate with líf. Homeric line-level μακρός + αἰών search returned no hit; not a claim of absence elsewhere.

The Homeric swift-foot formula was found outside the slab; the supplied Greek line carries a groaning casualty, and the Hittite partner is correspondence. Only foot is cognate with the external formula; replacement of the speed adjective cannot by itself establish inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Snow, frost and winds in a catalogue of harsh weather.
near_miss.why_not: Norse sníor/frost/uindar, Irish Reód/sneachta and Latin nix/uenti/pruinae supply genuine lexical parallels. However the lists differ in order, construction and purpose: eschatological catastrophe, personal exposure, and physical meteorology. These expected weather associations lack a distinctive shared formula. Irish Reód and sneachta are nouns in an enumeration; Welsh nyf is a negative/clitic sequence, and Sanskrit sneha is affection, not snow.

near_miss.lead: Growth or increase of superhuman strength versus μένος μέγα ... ἀέξει.
near_miss.why_not: Norse vex/ox/vaxit and Greek ἀέξει share growth vocabulary, but the belt increases strength, Fenrir grows, and wine restores a tired man. Ásmegin (neuter nominative singular subject) and afl are not cognate with μένος. The shared meaning is too ordinary to substantiate a renewed inherited formula.

near_miss.lead: Binding a dangerous being and being bound in a noose.
near_miss.why_not: Bundu/bundit and Vedic badhyase/baddha/badhyatām are cognate bind-verbs. Loki is tied with entrails and Fenrir with special fetters; the Vedic passages treat ritual bonds, curses or death. No second distinctive cognate constituent or matching figure is demonstrated; merely binding with bonds is insufficient.

The exact title has an external Homeric partner, recorded separately. The slab Vedic partners instead concern offerings and fathers approving gifts; neither predicates fatherhood of a ruler of gods and men. Snorri’s universal-creator wording also permits Christian or learned mediation.

near_miss.lead: Sleep at night, compared with sleepless nights.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse giant sleeps and snores; the Homeric speakers lie awake and Herodotus describes ordinary sleeping or an army at rest. Sleep/night cognates do not form the same distinctive construction or context.

near_miss.lead: Sitting at the doorway or in the middle of the house.
near_miss.why_not: Norse miðr describes the room’s location; Thor sits in the doorway as guard. Vedic mádhye níṣattaḥ duroṇé describes Agni installed centrally in a house. Armenian նստեալ and դուրս accompany sackcloth, ashes and fasting in a Christian penitential setting. The three passages do not share a single congruent relation of middle, sitting and door, despite inherited lexical material.

near_miss.lead: Body of the primordial being made into the world, particularly head into heaven.
near_miss.why_not: RV 10.90.14 provides the searched structural parallel, but the supplied partners concern dye, lifespan, a military route and wounded skin. No cross-branch slab anchor matches the cosmogony. The Norse and Vedic head/heaven nouns are not shown to be cognate; this remains a thematic search lead.

near_miss.lead: Putting a helmet on the head in the arming sequence.
near_miss.why_not: The Latin partner uses caput in plant propagation. Although Norse hofud and Latin capite are cognate, the Latin passage has no arming scene or helmet collocation; the scene alone does not justify a phrase claim.

search_lead.cognate: Norse faðer and Greek πατήρ continue *ph2tēr; guð/θεός and maðr/ἀνήρ are lexical replacements, not cognate pairs.
search_lead.argument: Norse faðer governs the coordinated genitives guðanna and manna, as Greek πατήρ governs ἀνδρῶν and θεῶν; both designate the chief god. Searched and verified in the Homeric treebank, also at Iliad 11.182. A strong title-level comparison for review, but the late prose explanation of Allfather expands to all created things and may reflect Christian or classical learning.

search_lead.cognate: Langr and dīrgha- continue the inherited long adjective (*dl̥h1gh-); líf and āyus are not cognate.
search_lead.argument: Norse langt lif is a neuter adjective+noun object allotted by the Norns; the Vedic objects are long life granted by divine benefactors. Corpus search confirms repeated Vedic wording. The allotment context is comparable, but ordinary wishing for longevity and lexical replacement make inheritance uncertain.

search_lead.cognate: Fót- and πόδ- continue *pod-; hvatr and ὠκύς are not asserted cognate.
search_lead.argument: Fothvataztr is fóthvatastr, nominative masculine singular superlative: Thjalfi is swiftest of men. Fóthuatur in the other slab passage is fóthvatr, nominative masculine singular, applied to Heimer. Greek accusative of respect plus swift is a recurrent heroic epithet. Search returned 39 Iliadic verse co-occurrences; the resemblance is conventional heroic diction but only one secure cognate component, not evidence sufficient for a claim.

search_lead.cognate: No secure cognate pair between Norse haus/himinn and Vedic śīrṣan/dyau- is established here.
search_lead.argument: The Norse gods make heaven from Ymir’s skull; Vedic heaven develops from the primordial being’s head (ablative śīrṣṇaḥ). Verified by a local RV text search. This precise body-part/cosmic-part correspondence merits thematic review, but without matching lexical material it is not an inherited-phrase claim. The surrounding Norse flesh/earth and bones/rocks equations must not be attributed to this Vedic verse.
